title: Linear Regression
text:
Interpretation

Generally

\(\hat{\alpha}\) is the intercept on the y-axis, the value that Y takes when X is zero. \(\hat{\alpha}\) is a constant, it doesn’t change and remains the same regardless of the value of X.
\(\hat{\beta}\) is the coefficient (or slope), the average change in Y for one unit increase in X. \(\hat{\beta}\) is always in terms of Y’s units.

To report your results, you can say something like: “On average, Y changes by \(\hat{\beta}\) [Y’s units] for a 1 [X’s unit] increase in X.”


Translated in this case
“Each additional prisoner per 100,000 people in the previous year is associated with an increase of 2.012 in the predicted violent crime rate per 100,000 people.”

title: Vectors and Vector Operations
text:
Vectors
A vector is a set of values of the same type. You can think of it like a column on a spreadsheet. We can make a vector with the c() function.








All the elements in a vector need to be the same datatype, there are some functions that work on entire vectors.
We can get the mean, or average, number of Red Bulls I drink every week for the last 6 weeks by using the mean() function.








Note that every element in redbulls_drank is of the numeric type. We can also do things with vectors filled with characters. The toupper() function turns every character into uppercase.








However, it wouldn’t make sense to try to get the mean of my favorite flavors. Nor would it make sense to try to uppercase numbers.








It also wouldn’t make sense to get the mean of the number of Red Bulls I drank and my favorite flavors.








This doesn’t mean that numeric vectors can only use numeric vector functions, that logical vectors can only use logical vector functions, and so on. The length() function tells you how many elements are in a vector, and works on all kinds of vectors, and the unique() function tells you how many unique values are in a vector.








You can also access a specific element in a vector based on its position. In redbull_flavor, “cherry” has a position of 1, “lime” has a position of 2, “apple” has a position of 3, and “strawberry” has a position of 4. We can refer to a specific element by: redbull_flavor[1], which is “cherry”









Vector to Vector Operations
We can work with multiple vectors. We’ll make a new numeric vector that lists the number of cups of water I drank each week for the past 6 weeks.








We can get a new vector by adding redbulls_drank to waters_drank using the same numeric operation rules for numerics.

title: Getting and setting working directory
text:
What does “Working Directory” mean?
Your working directory is the folder R is currently looking in. When you tell R to “open titanic.csv,” it only looks inside that one folder. If the file is in a different folder (like Downloads), R won’t find it, even though the file is on your computer.
We also want to be aware of what working directory we are currently in.


Getting working directory
We will use the getwd() function. getwd() stands for “get working directory.” It tells you which folder R is currently “standing in.”

Create a R code chunk in your markdown file
Type getwd(), and run the chunk.




What your markdown file should look like


The output is your current the folder path. - For Mac users, the output should look something similar to: /Users/name/Desktop/comm_106 - For Windows users, C:/Users/name/Desktop/comm_106






Windows users: check for OneDrive





If your Desktop is synced to OneDrive, your folder path will look like C:/Users/yourname/OneDrive/Desktop/comm_106 instead of C:/Users/yourname/Desktop/comm_106. Run getwd() to see which one you have.




For Posit Cloud users, it should be: “/cloud/project”



Set working directory
If your working directory isn’t your comm_106 folder, you can change it with the setwd() function. setwd() stands for “set working directory.” It tells R which folder to look in.

Copy the folder path of your comm_106 folder
In the Console (bottom left), type setwd("your folder path") and hit Enter

For example:


practice_01.qmd

```{r}
setwd("/Users/name/Desktop/comm_106")
```

Run getwd() again to double check that it worked.






Tip



Make sure to use forward slashes (/) in your path, not backslashes (\). Windows copies paths with backslashes, so you’ll need to switch them.




Load in the dataset
We’ll use the read_csv function from the tidyverse package to load our dataset (titanic.csv) in.
Copy and paste the following in your markdown file, and run the code


practice_01.qmd

```{r}
df <- read_csv("titanic.csv",  show_col_types = FALSE)
```

We’ll go over in detail what all of this actually means later, but the gist is that we just turned our csv into something we can actually work with in R.
If you got an error saying that “titanic.csv does not exist in current working directory,” it means that R looked in your working directory and didn’t find the file there. Usually this is because the file is saved somewhere else (like your Downloads folder), or because R is looking in a different folder than you think.
Make sure your titanic.csv is in your comm_106 folder. When you run code in a .rmd file, R looks in the folder the file is saved in, so keeping your data and your .rmd together means R can always find it.
Then run the read_csv chunk again.

title: Significance Tests
text:
The pieces we have so far are:

\(r\) We found a strong positive correlation between prison population and violent crime of 0.776.
\(\hat{\beta}\) We find that, for each additional prisoner per 100,000 people in the previous year is associated with an increase of 2.012 in the predicted violent crime rate per 100,000 people.

What we don’t have is a measure of how confident we are in our estimate of \(\hat{\beta}\). \(r\) is a measure of the strength of whether a line exists at all*, but it doesn’t tell us anything about the slope of the line. \(\hat{\beta}\) is the slope, but doesn’t tell us about the confidence with which we can say that the slope is that number exactly.

title: Histograms
text: To work through questions of distribution, we’ll use the dataset from Bertrand & Mullainathan’s 2004 study, “Are Emily and Greg More Employable Than Lakisha and Jamal? A Field Experiment on Labor Market Discrimination”. In this study, the authors sent out 4870 fake resumes, which they had randomly assigned to have either an African-American or White sounding name. They found that White names receive 50 percent more callbacks for interviews. The dataset, which you can download locally here, lists every resume and the job it was sent to.

title: Histograms
text:
Interpretation
Looking at the visual, we can see that the resumes are not uniformly distributed across years of experience, and that resumes generally have less years of experience.

title: Histograms
text:
Occupation
To think through this, we’ll make a bar plot for the occup_broad column, which categorizes the jobs a resume applied to into Executive, Administrative, Sales representatives, Sales workers, Secretaries, and Clerical. This makes it a nominal variable.








Compare this plot to the years of experience plot. In a histogram, the overall shape of the data tells us what the distribution of the data is, we can learn something about the data when our eyes move across the x-axis. In a bar plot of a nominal variable, the order of the x-axis doesn’t matter. You can rearrange the categories however you want and you’ll still have the same information. In the histogram, we can see that as years of experience increases, the less resumes there are.

title: Histograms
text:
Education
education lists the highest level of education reported on each resume, which ranges from: 1 = high school dropout; 2 = high school graduate; 3 = some college; 4 = College graduate or more, (and 0 for not reported). This makes it an ordinal variable, because the order of the categories matter.








At first glance, this seems to function very similarly as the years of experience histogram – we can see that (whatever distribution pattern)
However, the intervals on the x-axis are not equal. From the perspective of someone reading the resume, we can imagine that there is some difference in the evaluation of high school dropout applicants and high school graduate applicants. But is this difference the same as how someone with some college is compared to someone with a high school graduate?
More importantly, you can tell very different stories with the same data based on how you create categories, or even just choosing bin width.

title: Changing the Dataframe
text:
if_else()
We can also use conditional statements to generate new columns. Let’s say we want a column that indicates whether a passenger was an adult (Age >= 18)
We can use the if_else() function, which requires three inputs, in this order: (1) the condition (2) the value if the condition is met (3) the value if the condition is not met.









Dealing with unknown values
You may notice that some values in Is_Adult column are neither “Yes” or “No”, but something called NA instead. We get this value when the value in Age was missing, so R can’t determine whether or not the value is greater or equal to 18.
We can deal with this by adding another input into the if_else() function: missing = "Unknown"








Now, instead of NA as the value, the missing values will have an actual value.

title: Changing the Dataframe
text:
case_when()
if_else() is helpful when we only have two conditions, but we may have more than two.
